title: How Diabetes Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how diabetes works in the body. They cover statistics on rising type two diabetes, the simple sugar glucose and why cells need it, the pancreatic islets (beta cells making insulin and alpha cells making glucagon), and how the two hormones keep blood sugar in balance. They then describe the three types of diabetes (type one, type two, and gestational), their symptoms, and the physiological chain from insulin resistance to excess urination, thirst, thick blood, poor circulation, ketoacidosis, and hypoglycemia. The episode also covers prediabetes and reversibility (a small very-low-calorie diet study), common medications, glucose monitoring and apps, and pancreatic islet transplantation for type one. The episode ends with a listener mail segment correcting the Skyscraper episode about steel, iron, and foundations.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour dates
segments.summary: The hosts announce fall tour dates in Salt Lake City, Phoenix, and Melbourne, then complain about a dry How Stuff Works diabetes article and agree to make the topic fun.

segments.title: Diabetes statistics and prevalence
segments.summary: The hosts cite rising type two diabetes rates, around 30 million Americans with diabetes, about 84 million with prediabetes, roughly 327 billion dollars in annual costs, about 400 million worldwide, and it as a leading cause of death in the US.

segments.title: Glucose as cell fuel and homeostasis
segments.summary: Simple sugars and glucose are explained as the body's primary cell energy, absorbed from food through the intestine. The body keeps blood glucose at a steady level, and some cells, including brain cells, rely on glucose alone.

segments.title: Insulin and the pancreatic islets
segments.summary: Insulin is made by beta cells in the pancreatic islets when glucose rises after eating. It moves glucose into cells and directs liver and muscle cells to store glycogen and fat cells to store fat, and it also acts on amino acids and fatty acids. It also inhibits gluconeogenesis in the liver and kidneys.

segments.title: Glucagon and the opposite hormonal response
segments.summary: Glucagon, made by alpha cells in the pancreatic islets, does the opposite of insulin during fasting or sleep. It tells liver and muscle cells to break down glycogen and tells the liver and kidneys to make glucose, raising blood sugar back to normal.

segments.title: Normal blood glucose levels and testing
segments.summary: The ideal blood glucose level is about 90 milligrams per deciliter, or 5 millimolar. Home glucose meters use a test strip with glucose oxidase that turns blue, and the shade is analyzed. The word diabetes is linked to sweet urine from ancient tasting tests.

segments.title: Off-topic tangent on TV writing
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh talk about Chuck's past spec script writing, including a seventies show Halloween episode and a Simpsons spec, and about moving to Los Angeles.

segments.title: Types of diabetes: type 1, type 2, gestational
segments.summary: Type one, about five to ten percent of cases, is autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells, possibly triggered by a virus, and is often called juvenile or insulin-dependent diabetes. Type two, the most common, involves cells that resist insulin and is linked to obesity, and it is sometimes called insulin resistant diabetes. Gestational diabetes occurs during pregnancy and can raise later type two risk.

segments.title: Diabetes symptoms
segments.summary: Symptoms include excessive thirst, frequent urination, constant hunger, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, numbness in hands and feet, slow-healing wounds, and frequent infections. The hosts note many symptoms overlap with ordinary life.

segments.title: How high blood sugar causes symptoms
segments.summary: Glucose overloads the kidneys, causing frequent urination, dehydration, thirst, and thick blood. Thick blood leads to poor circulation, numbness, slow healing, infections, and gangrene. Ketoacidosis from fat breakdown can cause breath changes, heart and nervous system problems, and coma.

segments.title: Hypoglycemia and insulin shock
segments.summary: Too much insulin or insulin with too little food causes low blood sugar, leading to lightheadedness, shakiness, and in severe cases insulin shock and coma. Treatment includes juice or candy for quick sugar.

segments.title: Reversibility, treatment, and islet transplantation
segments.summary: A small study of thirty people on a very low calorie diet found many had normal fasting glucose after eight weeks and some stayed there after six months. Management covers diet, exercise, testing, oral medications for type two, and pancreatic islet transplantation as an experimental type one treatment that faces tissue rejection.
